Designing My AI Collaboration System

Without a coding background, I used UX methods to turn Claude into a collaboration system — building POCs to align the team, turning discussions into dev docs, and executing design files to my acceptance standards.

TeamHighFive Technology Co., Ltd.

[ What I want AI to solve ]

In the AI era, my daily work as a Product Designer looks like...

  • [1]

    Discussing needs, converging decisions

    Discussing PRDs with Claude; project context is written into a memory system, so any conversation can pick up where we left off

  • [2]

    Cross-discipline communication

    Producing clickable POCs without a coding background, deployed via Vercel as shareable links

  • [3]

    Executing design files

    Executing designs directly in Figma via MCP, following the brand identity and binding design tokens

  • [4]

    Design handoff

    A custom Skill applies my template and grows spec docs from project records — sorting rules, interaction states, field definitions, edge cases, and more

  • [5]

    Maintaining the design system

    My design standards are written as Skills — verifiable, syncable, repeatable

Why Claude?

Honestly, the starting point was simple: Claude was the tool my team provided. But "getting a tool" and "training it into a collaborative system" are two different things. What anchored me to Claude is my belief that what matters most in a designer's work are the "moments of convergence". I needed a discussion partner that asks me questions back and makes me articulate my decisions and reasoning.

[ In Practice ]

How does AI change the way my team and I talk?

[ Scenario 1 ]

POC: Helping the team communicate and align — no more meetings run on imagination

I don't have a coding background. Aligning on a feature idea used to mean static wireframes, lo-fi prototypes and verbal descriptions. Even after carefully syncing every stakeholder's needs, polished mockups still got scrapped and redone more than once.

ProductE-commerce supplier admin
BackgroundThe admin login mechanism was changing: redesign the sign-up/login and store-onboarding flows, and introduce two-factor authentication (2FA) to harden security. It also meant auditing the Owner’s sensitive actions and defining which ones still need a second check after login.
PurposeThis task was about optimizing an existing flow — the POC shows the differences from the old flow in one pass, including when 2FA is triggered in each scenario, keeping the team in sync.
Initial Prompt I want to build a POC demo simulating the scenarios that require 2FA login, plus the permission settings an Owner has after entering the platform ... .
Raise questions first if anything is unclear; finally deploy it via Vercel as a shareable link for the team.
When should 2FA appear? "Delete user" is a sensitive action that should trigger 2FA. Help me audit and tier the other actions too
Permission model & state conflicts Can one organization have multiple Owners? If only one, which combinations of the Owner's "active status" and "2FA binding status" actually conflict?

[ What is Changing ]

POC Deploy as a link Team discussion Finalize Into Figma

"Figma execution" became the final step of the process. We used to confirm requirements while endlessly revising mockups and prototypes; now ideas align and converge on the POC, and what gets drawn in Figma is already final. The cost of changing requirements went from "redrawing a mockup" to "editing a prompt".

What makes my POCs different from anyone else's?

My POCs feel like "the real product": they follow the brand's design system, consistency and tone; interactions behave realistically; even the mock data follows real business logic.

The difference comes from what I feed the AI: detailed design-system rules, my own acceptance standards, real usage scenarios, and more. The closer a POC is to reality, the sharper the team's feedback.

[ Scenario 2 ]

Design Docs: Growing specs from discussion records to cut post-handoff back-and-forth

"Ship the design first, backfill the spec later" — that's the reality of almost every handoff to engineering.
In larger teams, specs are written by PMs, maintained by design ops, and verified by QA; in a startup, a small team, or as a solo designer, all of those roles land on me. Before AI, documentation was always the thing I never had enough hands for.

INSIDE THE SKILL

design-prd-spec Design spec generation
Triggers Write me a design specWrite a PRDProduce a design specDocs to hand to engineering

How it runs

  1. 01Collect the inputs

    Asks for four required items first: feature name, where it lives in the product, request type, and a short summary. Optional: Figma link, ticket number, owner, timeline.

  2. 02Break the request down

    If a Figma link is given it reads the file directly, then works through six dimensions: pages and sections, component specs, sorting logic, interaction behaviour, edge cases, and anything API-related.

  3. 03Draft it

    Generates Markdown from the template into my docs folder, and prints the full draft in the conversation for me to read first.

  4. 04Publish once I approve

    Nothing goes out until I say yes; then it creates or updates the Confluence / Notion page over MCP.

Doc template v1.1 · 12 blocks

  • RequiredRevision history
  • RequiredRequest info
  • As needed0 · Key terms
  • Required1 · Overview & design goals
  • Required2 · Information architecture
  • Required3 · Page & section specs
  • As needed4 · Sorting & display logic
  • As needed5 · State machine
  • As needed6 · Notifications
  • Required7 · Edge case summary
  • As needed8 · Phasing
  • As needed9 · API contract

Writing rules correct, and usable by engineering as-is

  1. 01

    Tables firstComponent specs, edge cases and API decisions always go in tables, never prose.

  2. 02

    Three fixed columnsSection / spec / notes — and notes hold the rule, not filler.

  3. 03

    Spell out the fallback chain1 → 2 → 3, indented to show hierarchy, including what happens when there is no data.

  4. 04

    Edge cases get their own tableTwo columns, scenario and behaviour; never mixed into component specs.

  5. 05

    Be exact with wordingWrite Hide, not “disappears”; write “shows N by default, click loads N more”; for search, state the trigger, the scope and the match logic.

  6. 06

    The API section records decisions onlyProduct-level calls (pagination, data source, search method); implementation is left to backend.

  7. 07

    LanguageTraditional Chinese, with technical terms kept in English (Tab, CTA, banner, API, endpoint).

Non-negotiables

If there is a Figma file, read it before writing — never assume　·　Edge cases cover at least empty data, no search results and error states　·　Any sorting logic ships with its full fallback chain

[ What is Changing ]

Create a memory file Decisions written in as we go Skill applies the template A PRD grows out

Whenever a new feature kicks off, I create a matching memory file and write in discussions and decisions as we go. At handoff, the Skill reads that record plus the Figma file, then applies my doc template. The PRD doesn't start from a blank page — it "grows out of memory". Writing docs went from "recalling every decision" to "confirming every decision".

What else is the project memory file good for?

The memory file is a "record once, output many" source: the same discussion record can grow into a PRD, open Jira tickets, or produce Figma annotations pinned next to the design. Same memory, many outputs — it saves me a lot of time.

[ Scenario 3 ]

Design System: Teaching AI my acceptance standards — execute, verify, sync

Building and maintaining a design system takes heavy manual work: defining components, organizing tokens, aligning rules with engineers.
What you end up with is large and complex — costly to manage, hard to follow; once the team gets busy, the rules drift away from reality and need re-organizing all over again.

INSIDE THE SKILL

design-execution Design file execution
Triggers Execute this designUpdate this design fileMake the RWD versionsMust pass my standards

How it runs

  1. 01Pick the mode

    New build, edit an existing file, or RWD multi-size. When it is unclear: a Figma node-id in the request means edit mode.

  2. 02Load the platform rules

    Detects admin, customer-facing web or app, and reads that platform’s rule file before touching Figma; RWD adds breakpoint and Variable Mode mapping on top.

  3. 03In edit mode, read before touching

    Scans the existing nodes: node-id, variables already bound, whether it is a component instance, current auto-layout settings. Only the requested parts change — no rebuilding.

  4. 04Build and bind in one pass

    Variable IDs are sampled from already-bound nodes in the current file; every node gets its tokens the moment it is created, not patched in at the end.

  5. 05Audit before reporting done

    Runs the binding-coverage script; unbound counts must all reach zero, or be listed as documented exceptions.

Acceptance criteria all six, or it is not done — nothing gets reported half-met

  • A

    Token bindingColour, stroke weight, spacing and radius all bound to variables; IDs sampled from the current file, never hardcoded.

  • B

    Text stylesEvery TEXT node uses a text style; text colour bound to a colour variable.

  • C

    Component sourceButton / input / select / badge / icon always come from the library; switch variants with setProperties, never detach.

  • D

    Auto layoutEvery container uses auto layout; FILL sizing set after appendChild; no absolute positioning (overlays aside).

  • E

    Edit safetyOnly the requested scope changes; nodes that already carry variables get a new variable, not a raw colour value.

  • F

    Layer namingFollows the team convention; no leftover defaults such as Frame 1 or Rectangle 2.

Hard rules every one of these came from getting burned

  1. 01

    Never hardcodefills, strokes, strokeWeight, textStyle, padding, gap and radius are always bound to variables.

  2. 02

    Sample variable IDs on the spotToken IDs differ from file to file; IDs remembered from last time are not reused.

  3. 03

    Order mattersFILL sizing and setBoundVariable both have to come after appendChild.

  4. 04

    Do not reach inside instancesSwitch variants with setProperties rather than editing a child’s fill or font; detach only as a last resort.

  5. 05

    Verify as you goScreenshot or read metadata after each section, instead of finding out at the very end.

  6. 06

    When no token fitsBrand one-offs stay hardcoded and get listed in the report; spacing with no exact token takes the nearest step.

  7. 07

    Ask when unsureAnything ambiguous in the design comes back to me instead of being guessed.

Non-negotiables

No Figma edits until the rule file has been read　·　Binding audit reaches zero unbound, exceptions documented　·　If a component cannot be found, search the library — never draw it by hand

[ What is Changing ]

Execute custom rules Build nodes, bind tokens 100% binding audit New tweaks become rules Written back into the Skill

The AI's first output didn't pass: hard-coded colors, unbound spacing, and a dialog drawn as a plain card instead of using the component.

The difference: "every correction becomes a rule". Colors always bind to variables, dialogs always use library components, icons always Lucide — never emoji ... Make the same mistake twice and it becomes a permanent rule.
